items.followUp: State one difference between a scientific theory and a scientific law, and give an example of a biological law.

rubric.why: Explains how a theory is accepted as a law in the textbook account.
rubric.description: A theory is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence before it is accepted as a law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking repeated testing or verification with acceptance as a law.

rubric.why: Gives an example of a biological law.
rubric.description: Names a biological law, such as Mendel’s law of segregation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A theory that is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence may be accepted as a scientific law.
Mendel’s law of segregation is an example of a biological law.

items.followUp: Who discovered the malaria parasite, and where did he find it?

rubric.description: Laveran discovered that malaria is caused by a parasite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Laveran discovered the malaria parasite.

rubric.why: States where the parasite was observed.
rubric.description: He observed the parasite in the blood of malaria patients.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the blood of malaria patients as the place of observation.

modelAnswer: In 1880, Alphonse Laveran discovered the malaria parasite, Plasmodium.
He observed it in the blood of malaria patients.

items.followUp: Why is a control group used when testing the effect of a variable?

rubric.why: Identifies the control’s role as a basis for comparison.
rubric.description: A control provides a standard for comparison with the experimental group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it provides a comparison or standard.

rubric.why: Explains how comparison helps assess the experimental factor.
rubric.description: It helps determine whether the observed effect is due to the variable being tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the comparison to judging the effect of the tested variable.

modelAnswer: A control provides a standard for comparison with the experimental group.
This helps show whether a change in the results is due to the variable being tested.

items.followUp: What pigments give leaves their green colour and many petals their bright colours?

rubric.why: Identifies the pigment responsible for the colour of leaves.
rubric.description: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chlorophyll as the leaf pigment.

rubric.why: Explains why petals have colours different from leaves.
rubric.description: Petals contain other pigments, commonly in chromoplasts, which produce their colours.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying petal pigments or chromoplasts.

modelAnswer: Leaves are green because their cells contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
Petals contain other pigments, often in chromoplasts, which give them colours different from leaves.

items.followUp: Compare the shape and usual location of cuboidal and columnar epithelial cells.

rubric.why: States the characteristic shape of cuboidal epithelial cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their shape as cube-like.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the shape of columnar epithelial cells from cuboidal cells.
rubric.description: Columnar epithelial cells are tall and column-shaped, being longer than they are wide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cells as column-shaped or tall.

modelAnswer: Cuboidal epithelial cells are cube-shaped, with their height and width approximately equal.
Columnar epithelial cells are tall and column-shaped, with their height greater than their width.

items.followUp: What is meant by species diversity?

rubric.why: Captures the central idea of biodiversity as variety.
rubric.description: Biodiversity means the variety of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as variety among organisms.

rubric.why: Shows the range of organisms included in biodiversity.
rubric.description: It includes the diversity of species, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning species or examples of organism groups.

modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms found in an area or on Earth.
It includes the diversity of species, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.

items.followUp: Into which two kingdoms was Monera divided in the six-kingdom classification?

rubric.why: States the main change made to Whittaker’s classification.
rubric.description: Margulis and Schwartz modified the five-kingdom system by dividing Monera into two kingdoms, producing a six-kingdom system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Monera was split and the system had six kingdoms.

rubric.why: Names the two kingdoms formed by the division.
rubric.description: The two kingdoms were Archaebacteria and Eubacteria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both kingdoms.

modelAnswer: Margulis and Schwartz modified Whittaker’s five-kingdom classification by dividing Monera into two kingdoms, making six kingdoms.
The two kingdoms were Archaebacteria and Eubacteria.

items.followUp: How do viroids differ from viruses in their structure?

rubric.why: Identifies the basic structure of a viroid.
rubric.description: A viroid consists of a short, circular RNA molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is made of circular RNA.

rubric.why: Distinguishes viroids from viruses by the absence of a protein coat.
rubric.description: Viroids have no protein coat and consist only of RNA.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viroids lack a protein coat or consist only of RNA.

modelAnswer: Viroids are infectious agents made of a short, circular RNA molecule.
They have no protein coat and consist only of RNA.
